title: How to Deploy Multilingual Conversational AI in 2026?
summary: A step-by-step framework for deploying multilingual conversational AI across voice, chat, and email, with governance, testing, and localization practices.
body_text: You deploy multilingual conversational AI in five phases: audit language and channel scope, localize each language independently, build governance and escalation rules per language, test with native speakers before launch, then roll out one language at a time. Treating a second language as a translation setting instead of its own phased rollout is the single most common reason multilingual deployments underperform. Global customer support teams increasingly need one conversational AI agent deployment that works consistently across voice, chat, and email, in every language a customer might use, not five disconnected systems duct-taped together by channel. What's the step-by-step framework for launching multilingual conversational AI? The framework runs in five phases, in this order: Audit scope: List every language your customer base actually uses and every channel- voice, chat, email- they contact you on today. Don't guess; pull it from support tickets and call logs. Localize per language: Build out intents, tone, and native-sounding speech or text for each language independently, not as a translation pass over the primary language's build. Define governance: Set escalation rules, compliance requirements, and data residency per language and per region before any of it goes live. Test with native speakers: Run real, unscripted conversations in each language and channel, and fix what breaks before a customer finds it. Roll out incrementally: Launch one language at a time, monitor it, then move to the next, rather than launching everything simultaneously. Skipping straight to rollout after localization, without a governance or native-speaker testing phase, is where most multilingual deployments run into trouble after launch instead of before it. How do you localize a conversational AI agent across voice, chat, and email? You localize each channel separately, since the same language can need different handling depending on how the customer is communicating. Voice needs native-sounding text-to-speech and accurate speech-to-text for regional accents, not just correct vocabulary. Chat needs to match written conventions, formality level, and even punctuation habits that vary by language and region. Email needs a tone appropriate to a more formal, asynchronous format than either voice or chat. Customer experience automation breaks down fastest at the seams between channels. A customer who starts in chat in Spanish and later calls in should reach a conversational AI agent that remembers that context and continues naturally, not one that starts over because voice and chat were built as separate systems with separate localization work. What governance do global support teams need for multilingual AI? Global support teams need escalation ownership, compliance mapping, and data residency rules defined per language and per region before launch, not worked out reactively after a call goes wrong. Two governance gaps come up constantly: Escalation coverage: An agent that correctly identifies a call needs a human, then routes it to someone who doesn't speak the caller's language, has solved the easy half of the problem Compliance mapping: Data residency and consent rules aren't uniform across regions, and a setup compliant in one market isn't automatically compliant in the next The same warm transfer for Voice AI logic that carries context from AI to human on a single-language call matters even more here, since the human picking up the call needs both the conversation history and confirmation they're actually equipped to continue it in that language. How do you test a multilingual conversational AI agent before launch? You test it with native speakers running real, unscripted conversations in each language and each channel, not a translation review of the scripts. Vocabulary being technically correct doesn't mean an agent sounds natural, and a native speaker will catch stiff phrasing, wrong formality level, or an accent gap a translation check never surfaces. Test escalation paths specifically, not just the happy path. Confirm a flagged call or chat actually reaches a human who speaks that language, with full context attached, before the language goes live. The approach to reducing average handle time without firing your team applies just as directly here, since the coverage logic, letting AI clear routine volume so humans focus on what needs judgment, doesn't change based on which language the conversation is in. Why does customer experience automation depend on getting language right? Because language preference is one of the strongest predictors of whether a customer trusts a brand enough to engage with it in the first place. Unbabel's 2021 global multilingua l CX survey found that 68% of consumers said they'd switch to a different brand that offers support in their native language.A conversational AI agent that automates efficiently in English but sounds robotic or unnatural in a second language isn't actually delivering the automation win it looks like on paper. That gap tends to show up first in the metrics teams already track: resolution rate holding steady while CSAT quietly drops in a specific language, or deflection numbers looking fine while escalation volume in that language climbs. Tracking quality per language and per channel, not just in aggregate, is what catches this before it shows up as churn. This same consistency question extends to sales conversations, not just support. The playbook for using voice AI for lead generation covers how qualification logic gets built so it asks useful questions, and that same logic needs to work identically across every language a lead might call in on, not just the primary one. Getting started with your multilingual conversational AI deployment Run the five-phase framework on one additional language first: audit scope, localize per channel, define governance, test with native speakers, then launch. Confirm human escalation coverage exists in that language before going live, not after the first call that needs it. Once that first additional language is running well, the same five phases apply to the next one, and most of what's learned about testing and governance carries over rather than starting from zero each time. Voice AI agent SigmaMind is built to run voice, chat, and email through the same underlying agent, so expanding to a new language means repeating the localization and testing phases, not rebuilding the automation logic from scratch. Bottom line: multilingual conversational AI deployment succeeds or fails on process, not model quality. Audit scope, localize per channel, govern escalation and compliance per language, test with native speakers, and roll out one language at a time. title: Five Keys to Scaling an Innovation Culture
summary: As Alnylam’s clinical pipeline rapidly expands, I’ve found myself reflecting on what has enabled our progress and what it will take to achieve our ambitious 2030 goals.
body_text: Our News Share this: Five Keys to Scaling an Innovation Culture Broadly applicable lessons from biopharma July 20, 2026 Pushkal Garg, MD Chief Research and Development Officer, Alnylam Pharmaceuticals As Alnylam’s clinical pipeline rapidly expands, I’ve found myself reflecting on what has enabled our progress and what it will take to achieve our ambitious 2030 goals. When I joined the company in 2014, before our first commercial product, I was struck by a few aspects of our culture that felt different and essential to advancing a new class of medicines like RNAi therapeutics. In retrospect, they were foundational to our ability to innovate. Alnylam has changed in many ways, but those key aspects remain important as we grow. We have to be deliberate about protecting and strengthening them so we can continue to expand the reach of RNAi therapeutics to many more patients. The learnings also connect closely to our recently launched Leadership Expressions, a framework we developed to be intentional about how we lead, collaborate, make decisions, and innovate together, particularly as we add new team members. Scaling an innovation culture isn’t easy, but I believe it’s essential to achieving what we’ve set out to do. 1. Patients First Patients are absolutely critical to everything we do. And they’re critical to fostering innovation. In our world, the patient is the ultimate customer, and keeping that front and center gives us our “why,” a real sense of purpose that can motivate people on hard days. If you walk through our offices around the world, you’ll see walls filled with photos of patients we’ve helped or hope to help with our RNAi therapeutics. Because at the end of the day, that’s what matters, whether we make a difference for someone. It also sharpens the team’s focus. When you’re advancing a new therapeutic candidate, you should be able to answer a simple question: what unmet need does this fulfill? If you anchor on that, it really starts to crystalize the decisions, including who you enroll in a clinical study, what endpoints matter, and whether you’re set up to show meaningful benefit. This discipline becomes more important as you scale. There can be pressure at companies to “feed the beast” and chase blockbusters early. But early on, you have to keep the emphasis on unmet need and biologic conviction and let the market follow as you learn more. 2. Embrace Tension What we do is hard. It takes people with very different perspectives – scientists, clinicians, safety experts, commercial colleagues – all looking at the same problem from different angles. Those perspectives aren’t always aligned, and that’s a good thing. There should be tension. In fact, I worry when there isn’t some tension in the room because it usually means people aren’t speaking up. If people aren’t speaking up, then you’re not hearing the full picture. Early on at Alnylam, I was in plenty of meetings where the discussion got heated. Different leaders and functions had very different views on the same program, and we didn’t always agree. But there was trust, and everyone was working toward the same goal. Those moments weren’t a problem. They were the process. In many cases, that tension is what helped us sharpen our thinking and land on a better decision. That’s especially important as you scale, when the number of stakeholders increases and there’s a natural pull toward agreement instead of challenge. We need to guard against a culture of consensus, which can lead to compromises that produce weaker outcomes instead of the best choices. 3. Stay Bold As organizations grow, risk aversion often sets in. And in some ways, that’s natural. All of us are trained to look for problems and try to prevent them. That’s part of our job. And in drug development especially, the odds are against you. More things fail than succeed, so it’s easy to focus on all the reasons something might not work. You’re often making decisions with very limited information, sometimes based on early data from animal models, trying to understand what that will mean for patients. We’ve had to make decisions to move programs forward without knowing exactly how they would play out. That uncertainty can be uncomfortable, but if you wait until everything is de-risked, you’re going to miss opportunities to create something truly new. The other challenge is that as you get bigger, you add layers. And at every layer, there are more opportunities for someone to say no and put the brakes on a program, often for the right reasons. But over time, that can slow things down or stop good ideas from moving forward. So it’s important to keep an organization relatively flat and be thoughtful about saying no during scaling. Before you say no, ask yourself: is this a risk we should take? Because if you’re not taking smart risks, you’re probably not going to be very innovative. 4. Be Curious Curiosity is essential to innovation. If you’re trying to do something new, the answers aren’t written down anywhere. You have to go find them. And the only way to do that is to be curious – to talk to different people, to read widely, to connect dots across disciplines, and to look for examples in places you might not expect. One of the best examples of curiosity at work is our drug delivery platform. For the first 10+ years of the company, we were trying to answer a very basic question: how do you actually get the active ingredient of RNAi therapeutics into the right cells? It took years of trial and error and many people asking, “What else can we try?” to find a solution. It’s also really important to have a lot of humility in biopharma. We know a fraction of what there is to know about human biology, so you have to come in recognizing you don’t have all the answers. If you’re focused on being right all the time, you’re probably not listening, and you’re going to miss things that matter. So you want people who are curious, who ask questions, and who are open to learning. That’s how you ultimately uncover something new. 5. Activate Agency One of the most important things we can do is create a real sense of agency and accountability at all levels of the organization. Agency means people see themselves as co-owners. They’re not just operating within the four corners of their role, they’re looking for what needs to get done and stepping in to help solve it. That mindset shows up in moments that really matter. During the filing of our first RNAi therapeutic, we realized on a Friday that we needed to retrieve source data from clinical sites around the world or risk delaying approval. Within hours, people were stepping in and flying out over the weekend, working directly with sites. Nobody was thinking about roles. They just saw what needed to get done and took ownership. As organizations grow, it’s easy for people to stay in their lane or assume someone else will take care of something. You have to fight against that. Progress comes from people taking ownership, using their judgment, and navigating around obstacles to keep things moving. At the same time, we have to be clear that accountability sits with individuals. Decisions don’t get made by committees. People make decisions and own them. Taken together, these elements – putting patients first, embracing tension, staying bold, being curious, and activating agency – have helped Alnylam innovate over the long term. Whether you work in R&D or another area, I'd encourage you to consider: what does it take to build and sustain an innovation culture in your own team or organization? I'd love to hear what you think! Message me on LinkedIn . title: Sera Announces Publication Acceptance for PRIME Study
summary: Sera announced that the findings of the Prematurity Risk Assessment Combined with Clinical Interventions for Improved Neonatal OutcoMEs (PRIME) study were accepted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal.
body_text: The PRIME study, one of the largest studies on preterm birth, has been accepted for publication by a medical journal following abstract presentation earlier this year SALT LAKE CITY – Nov. 24, 2025 — Sera Prognostics, Inc. , The Pregnancy Company® (NASDAQ: SERA), focused on improving maternal and neonatal health by providing innovative pregnancy biomarker information to doctors and patients, today announced that the findings of the Prematurity Risk Assessment Combined with Clinical Interventions for Improved Neonatal OutcoMEs (PRIME) study were accepted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal. The PRIME study’s abstract data was selected as a late-breaking abstract for podium presentation earlier this year at the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine’s (SMFM) annual meeting. “We look forward to sharing PRIME manuscript data upon publication at upcoming medical meetings and through events with our research analysts,” said Zhenya Lindgardt, President and CEO of Sera Prognostics. About Sera Prognostics, Inc. Sera Prognostics is a health diagnostics company dedicated to improving the lives of women and babies through precision pregnancy care. The company’s PreTRM® Test is the only broadly validated, commercially available blood-based biomarker test for early, individualized risk prediction of spontaneous preterm birth. Sera Prognostics is headquartered in Salt Lake City, Utah. About The PreTRM® Test The PreTRM ® Test is the only broadly validated, commercially available blood-based biomarker test that provides an early, accurate and individualized risk prediction for spontaneous preterm birth in asymptomatic singleton pregnancies. The PreTRM ® Test measures and analyzes proteins in the blood that are highly predictive of preterm birth. The PreTRM ® Test permits physicians to identify, during the weeks 18 through 20 of pregnancy, which women are at increased risk for preterm birth and its complications, enabling more informed, personalized clinical decisions based on each woman’s individual risk. The PreTRM ® Test is ordered by a medical professional. Sera, Sera Prognostics, the Sera Prognostics logo, The Pregnancy Company, and PreTRM are trademarks or registered trademarks of Sera Prognostics, Inc. in the United States and/or other countries. title: Tractian Brings Asset Health Intelligence to Federal Agencies Through Knox's FedRAMP® High Authorization Platform
summary: Tractian now meets the highest bar in U.S. government security. Here's what that means for every organization that trusts us with its data.
body_text: Tractian now meets the highest bar in U.S. government security. Here's what that means for every organization that trusts us with its data. Tractian is now available to federal agencies through a FedRAMP® High authorized cloud environment, deployed in AWS GovCloud through our partnership with Knox Systems. This authorization clears some of the most rigorous security and data-handling standards the U.S. government defines, the same bar required to protect the most sensitive federal data in the country. The organizations that run critical operations - whether that means regulated industries, the mission readiness of the defense supply chain, or any environment where security is non-negotiable - can now hold Tractian to a standard that leaves nothing to assumption. What FedRAMP® High means FedRAMP® is the U.S. government-wide program that standardizes security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring for cloud services used by federal agencies. It certifies the environment an application runs in, the cloud itself, against strict federal data rules. Tractian runs in AWS GovCloud, the audited, access-restricted version of AWS built for government workloads, and holds authorization at the High baseline, the strongest level FedRAMP defines. High is what allows a system to support the full range of agencies and their most sensitive data categories. With the authorized environment in place, federal agencies can adopt Tractian without undertaking the lengthy authorization process typically required for new cloud environments. The same Industrial AI, now available to federal agencies This is not a commercial product wearing a badge. It is the same frontier of industrial AI already relied on across the Americas, now delivered under federal authorization. Data handling and deployment change. The intelligence does not. Tractian reads machine condition in real time and turns it into earlier warning, catching developing failures before they become downtime, so operations stay running and mission-ready. Deploy on your terms Security posture varies by mission, so deployment does too: GovCloud (FedRAMP® High): the default for most government and government-adjacent operations, running in the audited AWS environment for federal data. On-premise / edge: runs on the customer's own servers, with Tractian never accessing the environment, for when cloud is off the table. Air-gapped / disconnected: fully local, no internet connection at all, for the most restricted facilities. The deployment matches the environment, from a municipal utility to a fully disconnected facility. Your assets, your rules. Built to extend your team, not replace it Tractian extends what a team can see and anticipate. It does not replace the people who run the operation. Earlier warning, a fuller picture, and time to act. The decision, and the mission, stay with the operator. Continuous monitoring after authorization FedRAMP High authorized deployment is not a finish line. It is an ongoing commitment to continuous monitoring, security improvement, and meeting the evolving requirements of the organizations that depend on Tractian. As more of the industrial base modernizes how it protects critical assets, we're committed to delivering intelligence that is secure, adaptable, and built for the realities of the environments it runs in.

title: Leading with science, grounded in patient impact: Meet James Richardson, M.D.
summary: In this Newsroom article, Sarepta’s Chief Medical Officer shares why he left his career as a cardiologist to focus on developing treatments for rare diseases.
body_text: Clinical development engine As Chief Medical Officer at Sarepta, Dr. Richardson oversees several critical functions within the organization. He spends his days collaborating with colleagues across Research and Development, Medical Affairs, Patient Affairs and Regulatory Affairs. He also maintains ongoing communication with patient advocacy organizations and clinical trial investigators around the world. His role is centered on aligning the efforts of these diverse stakeholders toward a shared goal: delivering transformative therapies to as many patients as possible. Under his leadership, the Clinical Development team authors trial protocols, the detailed plan that explains how a medical study will be conducted to ensure it’s safe, fair and scientifically sound. The Biometrics team, also under his direction, conducts essential statistical analyses to evaluate the benefits of studies and assess potential risks. The Quantitative and Clinical Pharmacology group plays a critical role in translating preclinical findings into clinical strategies. They help determine appropriate dosing and interpret how biomarker data from animal models may predict outcomes in human trials. Additionally, the Safety group is responsible for monitoring safety in clinical trials, managing safety-related reporting, and overseeing the safety profile of marketed therapies. Together, these teams form the backbone of Sarepta’s clinical development engine, each one playing a vital role in advancing innovative therapies while upholding the highest standards of patient safety and scientific integrity. “Innovation and safety are the twin pillars of our mission,” says Dr. Richardson. “By harnessing the power of collaboration, we transform groundbreaking ideas into life-changing treatments—always with the patient’s well-being at the forefront of our efforts.” A personal connection For Dr. Richardson, this work is more than scientific, it’s deeply personal. To him patient-first means starting with a clear understanding of what matters most to the people living with these rare diseases. That close connection is one of the things he values most about working in rare disease and at Sarepta, in particular. Unlike the vast landscape of general medicine, the rare disease community is a close-knit circle where patients, healthcare providers, and industry partners often know each other by name and story. “As an industry professional working on common diseases, I often felt distant from patient outcomes due to the sheer number of patients and healthcare professionals involved,” he explains. “But in rare disease, my actions feel much more personal and directly connected to patient outcomes. There’s something very different about rare diseases—you can really know the community.”
